statement: In prospective population cohorts from the USA (one with Puerto Rico), Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand that measured cannabis use before age 18 and depression or anxiety later, adolescents in the highest category of use each study reported (mostly self-reported frequency in the past year or 6 months, such as weekly or daily use; in one study a cannabis use disorder by 17), compared with adolescents who did not use cannabis, had modestly higher odds of depression in young adulthood after adjustment for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety and other covariates chosen by each study: in a 2019 meta-analysis (Gobbi et al., 2019; AMSTAR 2 critically low) the pooled adjusted OR was 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; 7 studies; I2 0%), with every study's estimate above 1 (1.02 to 2.62) but only 2 of the 7 significant on their own, and 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67) without a cohort that overlaps with another. Anxiety did not clearly differ (OR 1.18, 0.84 to 1.67; 3 studies; I2 42%). No absolute risks were reported, and the review's figure of 7.2% of young-adult depression attributable to cannabis assumes that the link is causal, has no stated method and is not a result of its data. Which pooled estimates were adjusted for tobacco and other drugs cannot be checked from the article, and the authors say a strong causal inference cannot be made; they cite a propensity-score analysis in which the association became non-significant, and among 24 studies they could not pool, six found no association, one of them finding that males with more depressive symptoms went on to use more cannabis and linking later depression to tobacco rather than cannabis. Narrative reviews describe the link with depression as inconsistent and weaker than that with psychosis, with dose–response relations that lost significance after adjustment in one birth cohort (frequency of use by 16) and in the Swedish conscript cohort (heaviest use at 18), and relay an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies with OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94) and weak support for a causal explanation (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; second-hand); another links regular use with anxiety and depression without established causality (Volkow et al., 2014). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Teenagers who used cannabis most often were a little more likely to be depressed as young adults than teenagers who did not use it (about 1.4 times the odds, in 7 long-term studies), even after taking into account how they felt at the start. Anxiety did not clearly differ, but only 3 studies measured it. These studies cannot show that cannabis caused the depression: other differences between the teenagers may explain it, and in some studies the link disappeared after more careful adjustment.
population: Adolescents in prospective population cohorts in the USA (one with Puerto Rico), Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand, followed into young adulthood (11 pooled studies across all outcomes, 23,317 people)
exposure: Cannabis use before 18, mostly self-reported frequency in the past year or 6 months; the highest category each study reported (in one study a cannabis use disorder by 17)
comparator: Adolescents in the same cohorts who did not use cannabis (who could use alcohol, tobacco or other drugs)
outcome: Depression and anxiety in young adulthood (diagnostic criteria or scale cut-offs), adjusted at least for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety
magnitude: Gobbi et al. 2019, pooled adjusted odds ratios (random effects), highest reported use category against no use: depression 1.37 (95% CI 1.16 to 1.62; 7 studies; I2 0%; study estimates 1.44, 1.50, 1.10, 1.30, 1.48, 2.62 and 1.02); without the overlapping Victorian cohort 1.40 (1.17 to 1.67); by measure, structured diagnosis 1.38 (1.15 to 1.66) and scales 1.28 (0.83 to 1.97); by country, USA 1.54 (1.20 to 1.98) and other countries 1.24 (0.99 to 1.56); anxiety 1.18 (0.84 to 1.67; 3 studies; I2 42%). No absolute risks. Second-hand: an earlier meta-analysis of longitudinal studies, depressive disorders OR 1.49 (1.15 to 1.94), as relayed by Hall & Degenhardt 2009 and Hall 2015.

evidence.extracted: Inclusion: peer-reviewed original articles with prospective population-based data; cannabis use assessed before 18 and depression, anxiety or suicidality in young adulthood (18 to 32), controlled for at baseline; odds ratios adjusted at least for age, sex and baseline depression and/or anxiety; the report with the longest follow-up per cohort. By the authors' account, parental education, socioeconomic status, alcohol and smoking were also controlled in almost all included studies, while their Limitations say not all studies adjusted for other drugs or cigarettes (study card reporting issue).

evidence.locator: Cannabis use and other mental disorders, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: As summarized: in longitudinal studies since 1993 the relationship between regular cannabis use and depression has been weaker than that with psychosis; in the Swedish cohort depression was 1.5 times more common with the heaviest use at age 18 than in people who did not use cannabis, no longer significant after adjustment for confounders; a dose–response between frequency of use by age 16 and depressive disorder (Fergusson & Horwood) was no longer significant after adjustment; a meta-analysis found a modest association (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.94) and weak support for a causal hypothesis, because most studies had not adequately controlled confounders or excluded depressed young people being more likely to use cannabis; a combined analysis of four Australasian birth cohorts drew similar conclusions.

evidence.locator: Cannabis and mental health, 4th paragraph (left column)
evidence.extracted: As summarized: non-consistent and weak associations between cannabis use and depression; a dose–response between frequency of use at age 16 and depressive disorder was not significant after adjusting for confounders (Fergusson and Horwood); a meta-analysis reported OR 1.49 (95% CI 1.15 to 1.94) for depressive disorders, but its investigators argued that the studies had not controlled for confounders or excluded the possibility that depressed young people are more likely to use cannabis.

evidence.locator: ADVERSE EFFECTS › RELATION TO MENTAL ILLNESS, 1st–2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: As summarized: regular use is linked to a higher risk of anxiety and depression, without established causality (citing one cohort study); the authors add that factors predisposing to both use and mental illness make it difficult to attribute the increased risk to marijuana.

risk_of_bias.note: Adjusted for age, sex and baseline depression or anxiety, but adjustment for tobacco, other drugs, childhood adversity, family history and peer factors varies by study and cannot be checked from the article; a propensity-score analysis found no significant association; exposure self-reported; AMSTAR 2 critically low (card sc_gobbi_2019). Residual confounding, or depression leading to cannabis use, could change an odds ratio of this size materially.

inconsistency.note: No detectable heterogeneity in the depression pool (I2 0%); all seven estimates above 1.

indirectness.note: Worded for the contrast pooled (highest reported use category against none) and the outcomes measured.

imprecision.note: The depression interval is reasonably narrow, but the anxiety estimate rests on 3 studies with an interval from 16% lower to 67% higher odds, so the absence of a link with anxiety is not shown; only 2 of the 7 depression studies were significant on their own.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not downgraded separately.

dose_response.note: Not analysed: only the highest category was pooled; the narrative reviews relay dose–response relations that lost significance after adjustment.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: very low, the floor; the depression association alone would also be very low because of the risk-of-bias downgrade. Rated for the adjusted association as worded; whether cannabis use causes depression is not established by these sources, and the review's attributable-case figure is not used. Status replicated: seven cohorts, at least six of them independent (the Victorian cohort overlaps with the Australasian consortium), point the same way. The earlier meta-analysis relayed by both Hall reviews covers adolescents and adults and may share cohorts with this one; it is second-hand and not counted as independent replication, and the two Hall reviews, by the same author, describe the same studies.
